name: Asuba
title: Caleb's wife and matriarch in the line of Judah
lifespan: Unknown, early in the history of the tribe of Judah
summary: Asuba is a woman mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chronicles. She was the wife of Caleb, son of Hezron, and thus belongs to one of the earliest generations in the tribe of Judah – Hezron was the grandson of the patriarch Judah himself. Asuba bore three sons to Caleb: Jered, Shobab, and Ardon (1 Chron 2:18–19). Her Hebrew name ('Azuvah, עֲזוּבָה) means 'forsaken' or 'desolate'. After Asuba died, Caleb took Ephrath as his wife, and she bore Hur – ancestor of, among others, Bezalel, the skilled craftsman who oversaw the decoration of the tabernacle. It is worth noting that this Caleb is not identical to the more well-known Caleb, son of Jephunneh, who was one of the spies in Canaan. The text in 1 Chron 2:18 also raises textual-critical questions about the relationship between Asuba and the otherwise unknown Jerioth, showing that even brief genealogical notes can contain complex interpretive issues. Asuba's place in the genealogy marks an important branching point in the tribe of Judah and highlights how women in these lists function as connecting points for the various lines of the tribe.
roles: matriarch in the tribe of Judah

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in Caleb's genealogy
keyEvents.description: Asuba is mentioned as Caleb's wife in the genealogical record of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chronicles. The text introduces her in connection with the listing of Caleb's descendants through the line of Hezron.

keyEvents.title: Mother of three sons
keyEvents.description: Asuba bore the sons Jezher, Shobab, and Ardon to Caleb. These sons represent a distinct branch of Caleb's descendants, separate from the children he had with his other wife Ephrath.

keyEvents.title: The Death of Azubah and Caleb's New Marriage
keyEvents.description: After Azubah's death, Caleb married Ephrath, who bore him Hur. This transition marks the beginning of a new and significant branch of Caleb's lineage that includes Bezalel, the craftsman of the tabernacle.

versions.summary: Azubah was the wife of Caleb, son of Hezron, and mother to several sons. She is mentioned in 1 Chronicles as part of the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. Her name means 'forsaken' or 'desolate,' and she is primarily known through her connection to Caleb and his descendants.
versions.title: Caleb's Wife
versions.reason: [major] Caleb, son of Hezron, lived in the patriarchal period/early Israelite history. Hezron was a grandson of Judah, which places this Caleb (not to be confused with Caleb, son of Jephunneh, who was the spy) in the era around the patriarchs or the Exodus, not the time of the judges. The epoch should be set to 'patriarchs' or possibly 'exodus'.; [major] Caleb, son of Hezron, belongs to a much earlier generation than 1400 BC. Hezron was a grandson of Judah, son of Jacob, which places him closer to around 1800-1700 BC. The time indication should be adjusted.; [minor] The title should specify which Caleb is being discussed, since there are several Calebs in the Bible. 'Caleb's wife (son of Hezron)' or similar would have been more precise.; [minor] The claim that Azubah is 'part of the messianic line leading to King David and further to Jesus Christ' is theologically imprecise. The messianic line from Judah to David goes through Perez → Hezron → Ram → Amminadab (see 1 Chr 2:9-10, Ruth 4:19-22), not through Caleb (son of Hezron). Azubah belongs to a side branch of the tribe of Judah.; [minor] The role 'matriarch' may give the impression of a more prominent role than the text suggests. 'Ancestress in the tribe of Judah' or simply 'wife and mother' could have been more fitting.; [minor] The summary is well formulated, but it should be clarified that this Caleb (son of Hezron) is not the same as Caleb, son of Jephunneh, who spied out Canaan.; [minor] There are no footnotes about the linguistic meaning of the name, the difference between the two Calebs in the Bible, and the context of the genealogy in the books of Chronicles.

versions.summary: Azubah was the wife of Caleb, son of Hezron, and mother to several sons. She is mentioned in 1 Chronicles as part of the genealogy of the tribe of Judah (1 Chron 2:18–19). Her name means 'forsaken' or 'desolate' in Hebrew. This Caleb should not be confused with Caleb, son of Jephunneh, who was one of the spies sent to Canaan. After Azubah's death, Caleb took Ephrath as his wife, who bore Hur. Azubah is primarily known through her place in the genealogical record of the tribe of Judah and as a matriarch of a branch of that tribe.
versions.title: Caleb's Wife (son of Hezron)
versions.reason: [major] Caleb, son of Hezron, does not belong to the patriarchal period. Hezron was a grandson of Judah, and this lineage is traditionally placed in the period before or during the sojourn in Egypt, but in biblical chronology, Hezron's descendants are often linked to the period around the exodus/conquest. More precisely, this is a figure from the early genealogies of the tribe of Judah. The 'Patriarchs' era normally covers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. A more fitting era would be 'conquest' or possibly 'judges', since Hezron's lineage extends from the time in Egypt onward.; [major] Dating Asuba to "c. 1800–1700 BC" places her in the patriarchal period, which is too early. Hezron was a grandson of Judah, Jacob's son. Even with traditional chronology, Hezron's descendants would have lived closer to c. 1500–1400 BC or later. The dating should be adjusted.; [minor] The summary is good and informative but should be rephrased somewhat to distinguish it more from version 1 and avoid similar wording. The phrasing "was wife of Caleb, son of Hezron, and mother of several sons" is very similar to version 1.; [minor] The three events largely overlap and in practice cover only two verses (1 Chr 2:18–19). For such a brief biblical mention, three events are acceptable, but it may seem somewhat inflated. Nevertheless, the events work as they are.; [minor] The fourth footnote regarding the interpretive question about Jeriot is valuable and relevant. It would have been nice to also include a note on the genealogical significance of Caleb (son of Hezron) being linked to the Davidic line through Hur and Bezalel, but this is a suggestion rather than a deficiency.

versions.summary: Asuba is known from the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chronicles as the wife of Caleb, son of Hezron. She bore Caleb sons named Jered, Sobab, and Ardon (1 Chron 2:18–19). Her Hebrew name ('Azuvah) means 'forsaken' or 'desolate'. After her death, Caleb married Ephrath, who gave birth to Hur. This Caleb must not be confused with Caleb, son of Jephunneh, the well-known spy from Canaan. Asuba's place in the genealogy testifies to her role as a matriarch of an important branch of the tribe of Judah, a lineage that later includes significant figures such as Bezalel, the craftsman behind the tabernacle.
versions.title: Caleb's Wife (son of Hezron)
versions.reason: [major] Caleb, son of Hezron, belongs to the early period of the patriarchs/genealogies in the tribe of Judah, not the conquest era. The conquest era ('conquest') is associated with Caleb, son of Jephunneh. Caleb, son of Hezron, belongs to an earlier generation in the genealogy and should be placed in the 'patriarchs' epoch or possibly 'judges'. Since Hezron was a grandson of Judah (1 Chr 2:5,9), this Caleb belongs to the patriarchal period.; [major] The time indication 'ca. 1500–1400 BC' fits better with the conquest era and Caleb, son of Jephunneh. Caleb, son of Hezron, was much earlier in family history – Hezron was a grandson of Judah. A more accurate indication would be 'Unknown' or a vague reference to the patriarchal period, since exact dating is very uncertain.; [minor] The title is functional but could be made slightly more informative by clarifying that this concerns the genealogy in Chronicles.; [minor] The summary is good, but with two earlier versions scoring 5, the text should be further improved with more contextual depth and avoid similarities with previous versions. The text should also reflect the corrected epoch and avoid time indications linked to the conquest era.; [minor] The events are correct and have proper Bible references (bookId 13 = 1 Chronicles), but could possibly be combined into fewer events since everything stems from just two verses.; [minor] The footnotes are good and cover many aspects. The fourth footnote about the Jeriot problem is especially valuable and shows good textual critical awareness.

footnotes.text: The name Azubah (Hebrew: עֲזוּבָה, 'Azuvah) is derived from the verb 'azav' (עזב), meaning 'to leave' or 'to forsake.' The name can be translated as 'forsaken' or 'desolate.' Such names were not uncommon in ancient Israel and may have had various cultural or circumstantial explanations related to the child's birth.

There are two individuals named Caleb in the Bible: Caleb, son of Hezron (1 Chron 2:18), who was Azubah's husband, and Caleb, son of Jephunneh (Num 13:6), the well-known spy. Although some scholars have attempted to link them genealogically (cf. 1 Chron 2:49), most treat them as separate individuals with different positions in family history.

The genealogies in 1 Chronicles (chapters 1–9) were likely compiled after the Babylonian exile to restore tribal identities. Women mentioned in these records—such as Azubah—often mark important branching points in family lines and highlight inheritance rights among various branches of a tribe.

The Hebrew text of 1 Chron 2:18 is textually challenging. The relationship between Azubah and Jerioth is unclear—it is debated whether Jerioth was another wife, a daughter of Azubah, or if 'Jerioth' is an alternate name for Azubah herself. The Septuagint and the Masoretic Text offer somewhat different readings, and the question remains open among scholars.

Through Caleb's second wife Ephrath (also called Ephrata), Hur was born, who according to tradition was the grandfather of Bezalel—the craftsman behind the construction of the tabernacle (Exod 31:2). This lineage connects Caleb's descendants both to the Bethlehem area (cf. Ephratha/Bethlehem in Gen 35:19) and to central figures in Israel's cultic history.

Hezron, Caleb's father, was a son of Perez and grandson of Judah (1 Chron 2:5,9). This places Caleb, son of Hezron, very early in the history of the tribe of Judah—in generations shortly after the patriarch Judah himself. Precise chronological placement is difficult, as the genealogies in Chronicles may contain compressed generations.
